title: Chasing the Light
excerpt: On working with whatever the weather gives you, and why I stopped bringing a lighting kit to editorial shoots.
intro: Every photograph I have ever loved was made with light I did not control. This is a note on surrender — on arriving early, watching longer, and letting the room decide.

body.text: For years I travelled with a case of strobes and a bag of modifiers, convinced that control was the same thing as quality. The turning point came on a grey afternoon in Lisbon, when the power in our rented studio failed and we had forty minutes of window light to make the story work. Those frames outlived everything else we shot that week.

The useful skill is not reading light — it is patience. I now arrive ninety minutes early to every location and spend the first hour not photographing at all. I watch where the sun will land, which walls hold shadow longest, where the floor goes bright. By the time the subject arrives, the room has already told me where to stand.
The room has already told me where to stand. My job is to have listened.

None of this is romantic in practice. It means cold mornings and a lot of frames that fail. But the failures cost nothing, and the frames that work carry something a strobe cannot fake: the feeling that the photograph happened rather than was made.
